content.title: What is TGT Full Form? Meaning, Eligibility & Teacher Career Guide
content.text: TGT Teacher Eligibility, Salary, and Career Scope ExplainedTGT is the short form for Trained Graduate Teacher. This title is widely used in India’s educational sector to refer to teachers who are qualified to teach students of classes 6 to 10 (secondary level) in recognized schools. A TGT holds a graduation degree as well as a compulsory teacher training qualification. The term is essential for students preparing for teaching careers, as well as for those seeking a clear distinction between different teaching designations in schools. Meaning & Significance of TGT Trained Graduate Teacher (TGT) describes a professional who has completed a graduation (bachelor’s degree) in a relevant subject along with a certification in teaching such as B.Ed (Bachelor of Education). TGTs are directly involved in imparting subject-based education to adolescent students, preparing lesson plans, evaluating assignments, and creating a supportive classroom environment. TGT is not a separate course but a title/designation granted to those who hold the necessary qualifications and training to teach classes 6 to 10. Their primary role includes building fundamental academic knowledge in students and guiding them through secondary-level studies. How TGT Is Used Across Contexts In Indian education, TGT denotes eligibility for middle and secondary school teaching jobs in government, aided, and private schools. Only candidates with a graduate degree and an approved teaching certification (usually B.Ed) are eligible to appear for recruitment examinations for TGT positions. Teaching councils and educational boards specify TGT as the required standard for hiring teachers for specific subjects such as Science, Social Studies, Mathematics, English, and regional languages in classes 6–10. Beyond education, the abbreviation 'TGT' may have other uses globally, but in the Indian context, it refers strictly to the teaching profession. Key Differences: TGT, PGT, and PRT In schools, teachers are classified by the classes and subjects they teach. Below is a comparative table to help understand the main distinctions between TGT, PGT, and PRT designations. Criteria TGT PGT PRT Full Form Trained Graduate Teacher Post Graduate Teacher Primary Teacher Classes Taught 6th to 10th 11th & 12th 1st to 5th Minimum Qualification Graduate + B.Ed Post Graduate + B.Ed Graduate + D.El.Ed/B.Ed Key Responsibilities Teach secondary subjects,plan lessons/evaluate work Teach senior secondary subjects,guide for competitive exams Teach all core subjects,build foundation skills Private School Salary ₹25,000–₹40,000 ₹30,000–₹60,000 ₹15,000–₹30,000 Government School Salary ₹15,000–₹35,000 ₹25,000–₹50,000 ₹10,000–₹25,000 Eligibility & Qualifications for TGT A graduation degree in the relevant teaching subject (minimum 50% marks) Bachelor of Education (B.Ed) degree from a recognized institution Some schools may require a pass in CTET/STET as per norms Proficiency in English and Hindi is often preferred Practical Example Suppose a student completes a B.Sc. in Mathematics, followed by a B.Ed. degree. This student becomes eligible for TGT Mathematics posts in schools, where they can teach Mathematics from class 6 to 10. If they later complete an M.Sc. and wish to teach higher classes (11-12), they must target PGT roles. TGT Salary & Career Growth TGT teachers in private schools usually earn between ₹25,000–₹40,000 per month, while those in government schools may earn ₹15,000–₹35,000 per month. Allowances such as DA, HRA, and MA are also included in most government positions. Pay scales vary with experience, school type, and promotion opportunities. Senior TGTs may progress to administrative or PGT roles with higher studies and experience. Why Is TGT Important? TGT teachers play a crucial role in shaping the educational foundation and academic discipline of secondary students. They help students master subject concepts, develop analytical skills, and transition smoothly into higher secondary education.
